An interesting result is that the electricity generation from VRE tends to have more significant and variable changes from year to year compared to electricity demand. This is because electricity is primarily used for non-weather-dependent services such as industry consumption, household lighting and appliances, and other commercial and corporate activities. The weather-driven variations on the demand side are explained by changes in electric heating and cooling demand due to variation in temperatures and change in the cooling and heating system's efficiency, which is affected by temperature and humidity conditions.15

We use a representation of the power sector in 2030 that is aligned with the mix anticipated by the NECP19 plans. The REPowerEU scenario we analyze uses an updated mix, with solar, wind, heat pumps and EV capacities matching targets declared in the REPowerEU plan. Our HDD model represents the temperature-sensitive gas demand in the power, residential, and commercial sectors and clusters 40 historical CYs16 into four different temperature scenarios – mild, normal, hard, and hardest. Combining the impact of weather on VRE with the electricity generation from nuclear, other RES, and non-gas fossil technologies (oil and coal), we first estimate the impact of annual temperature variations on gas demand in the power sector (see Fig. 6).

Finally, a statistical analysis of temperature clusters17 shows that mild and hard years are common. The frequency of each temperature scenario across our CYs dataset was 30% mild, 49% normal, 21% hard, and 2.5% hardest (i.e., 1 in 40 years). We can, therefore, conclude:

1. Temperature changes from normal are not episodic, and their relation to the power system requires significant risk management resources: the relative difference from the baseline (normal temperatures) is significant in the hardest (+84%) and mild (−25%) CYs.
4.2. Implications for the EU's energy security

The EU significantly reduced pipeline gas imports from Russia, from 132 bcm in 2021 (BP, 2022) to 62 bcm in 2022 (Energy Institute, 2023). However, its dependence on Russian gas is still not insignificant – both pipeline and LNG from Russia amounted to 80 bcm in 2022, representing 23% of the EU's 2022 consumption (Energy Institute, 2023). : As a result of the nuclear accident in 2011, Japan switched off all of its nuclear reactors, increasing its demand for fossil fuels, primarily LNG. This increased annual LNG imports by 17.6 bcm (+18%) from Japan in 2012, representing about a quarter of the global spot and short-term LNG volumes (Hayashi and Hughes, 2013). The sudden increase in demand led to a shift in the global gas market balance, with a period of tightness supported by increased demand and constrained by supply growth. As a result, gas prices increased by at least 50% during the three years following the accident (see Fig. B7).

: The record-high prices in the EU (see Fig. B8) reduced its natural gas consumption by 55 bcm in 2022 compared to 2021 – the steepest decline in absolute terms in history. This demand reduction was due to fuel switching, energy efficiency, and behavioral changes in the residential and commercial sectors. But, it also led to production curtailments in energy-intensive industries, reducing the industrial demand by 22 bcm (Zeniewski et al., 2023). The economic situation led to high inflation in the EU, reaching 11.5% year-on-year in November 2022 and 9.9 % in February 2023. Energy and food prices experienced the highest increase (+15%), impacting poorer communities harder and leading to social unrest and strikes.
